lessons.title: ਅੱਖ (akkh) — the eye that kept both its consonants
lessons.gloss: eye — a doubled consonant that survived whole, so it never had a tone to lose

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. segments.text: ਭੈਣ closed a chapter about people. This chapter checks on how someone is — starting with the parts of the body a friend might actually ask about.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਅੱਖ — akkh — eye.
ਅ, the bare vowel-carrier for a, then the ੱ addak — the same doubling mark from ਰੱਬ and ਦੁੱਧ — over ਖ kh. Read together: a-kkh, the k held and released with real force, not a tone standing in for it.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a doubled consonant that never traded itself for pitch

segments.text: akkh is inherited from Prakrit akkhi, from Sanskrit akṣi, "eye," from Proto-Indo-Iranian Hákši, from Proto-Indo-European h₃ókʷs — unbroken all the way to English eye itself.

Every tone you have met so far came from a consonant that lost something — its breathy voice, or the whole of itself. ਖ here loses nothing: Sanskrit akṣi's consonant cluster became a doubled kkh in Middle Indo-Aryan, and Punjabi still says both halves in full. That is exactly why akkh is flat — the addak mark you are reading is the opposite move from a tone mark: it doubles a sound that survives, where a lost sound is what leaves a tone behind. Hindi took a different road with the same word, smoothing the cluster down into a nasal vowel, āṅkh — no doubling, no tone, a third outcome entirely.

segments.instruction: akkh — eye — the kkh held, not a tone
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **akkh** — eye — the *kkh* held, not a tone]

segments.instruction: PIE h₃ókʷs becomes Sanskrit akṣi becomes ਅੱਖ (akkh), and becomes English eye
a doubled consonant that survives (akkh) against one that vanished into tone (bharā's bh)

lessons.title: ਕੰਨ (kann) — a false friend hiding in plain sight
lessons.gloss: ear — a word that looks like it hides "to do" inside it, and does not

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say madad karnā, "to do a favour of help," and pull its stem apart: kar-. Watch that same string of sounds turn up again, meaning something it has nothing to do with.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਕੰਨ — kann — ear.
ਕ k, ੰ the ṭippī nasal, ਨ n — and the vowel is nasalized where ਅੱਖ (akkh) doubled a consonant instead. Ka-nn, with the doubling this time carried by the nasal mark rather than the addak.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — not the verb it resembles

segments.text: ਕੰਨ (kann) is inherited from Sanskrit karṇa, "ear." Its own root beyond Sanskrit has never been securely traced — one guess ties it to a word for "twisting" or "winding," another to a word for "point," and no source picks a winner.

Here is the trap: karṇa looks exactly like it is hiding ਕਰਨਾ karnā, "to do," the very verb inside ਮਦਦ ਕਰਨਾ. It is not. Karnā, "to do," traces to a completely different Proto-Indo-European root, kʷer-. Karṇa, "ear," does not connect to it at all — the resemblance is a coincidence of sound, the kind every language accumulates, and Punjabi keeps both words close enough in spelling that a learner has to be told, not left to guess.

segments.instruction: is kann related to karnā, "to do"? (No — a coincidence of sound.)
segments.source: [YOU STATE: is *kann* related to *karnā*, "to do"? (No — a coincidence of sound.)]

segments.instruction: madad karnā's own kar-, and how it differs from kann's
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: *madad karnā*'s own **kar-**, and how it differs from *kann*'s]

segments.text: Give the word for "ear." (Kann.) Does it share a root with karnā, "to do"? (No — different Proto-Indo-European roots entirely.) Name the two body words so far. (Akkh, kann.)
Sources: Wiktionary: ਕੰਨ (kann); Wiktionary: Sanskrit karṇa.

segments.prompt: Does kann, 'ear', share a root with karnā, 'to do'?

feedback.correct: Right: karṇa 'ear' and karnā 'to do' trace to different roots entirely — the resemblance is only in the sound.
feedback.incorrect: No. karṇa 'ear' and karnā 'to do' come from unrelated roots; they only sound alike.

lessons.title: ਮੂੰਹ (mūnh) — a consonant that wore all the way down to a tone
lessons.gloss: mouth, face — the second word this book has found with a level high tone

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called The letters in this word and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: ਚਾਹ's final ਹ was not really a consonant — it marked a level high tone, because the word ended right there. This word ends the same way, from a consonant that used to be something else entirely. And unlike ਕੰਨ (kann), which only looks like it hides ਕਰਨਾ inside it, this word hides no false friend at all.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਮੂੰਹ — mūnh — mouth, also face.
ਮ m, ੂ long ū, ੰ the nasal ṭippī, ਹ — again not spoken as h, marking the same level high tone you first read in ਚਾਹ: mū́h̃.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — kh wore down to h, then h wore down to nothing

segments.text: mūnh is inherited from Sanskrit mukha, "face, mouth" — Punjabi also kept the same word a second time, whole, as the learned borrowing ਮੁਖ mukh, the way it kept both ਪਸੰਦ and its own inherited relatives side by side before.

On the inherited path, mukha's middle kh did not simply vanish. Middle Indo-Aryan first softened intervocalic kh down to a plain h — a regular, well-worn move, nothing to do with the breathy-voiced letters that gave you bharā's low tone or samajhṇā's falling one. Punjabi then lost that h too, the same way it lost cāh's Persian-final one, and let its pitch land on the vowel before it: level and high, because — exactly as in cāh — nothing follows it in the word.
So mūnh and cāh reach a level high tone from different histories — one from a worn-down kh, one from a borrowed word's own h — and arrive at the identical sound.

segments.instruction: mūnh — mouth, face — level and high
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **mūnh** — mouth, face — level and high]

segments.instruction: Sanskrit mukha becomes kh softens to h becomes h is lost becomes ਮੂੰਹ (mūnh)
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: Sanskrit *mukha* → *kh* softens to *h* → *h* is lost → **ਮੂੰਹ**]

segments.instruction: the learned twin of mūnh that kept the whole word intact

segments.text: What tone does mūnh carry, and which earlier word — not a body word, but the same pattern — first showed it? (Level high; cāh, tea, from Chapter 10.) What softened before Punjabi lost it entirely in mukha becomes mūnh? (Kh, first to plain h.)
Sources: Wiktionary: ਮੂੰਹ (mūnh); Wiktionary: Sanskrit mukha.

segments.prompt: What Sanskrit word does mūnh come from, and what learned Punjabi word keeps the same source intact?

feedback.correct: Right: both come from Sanskrit mukha — mūnh worn down by sound change, mukh borrowed later as a learned whole.
feedback.incorrect: Sanskrit mukha, kept whole a second time as the learned borrowing mukh.

lessons.title: ਨੱਕ (nakk) — the whole face, run back
lessons.gloss: nose — the plainest possible cousin of the English word for the very same part

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called The letters in this word and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: ਅੱਖ (akkh), ਕੰਨ (kann), ਮੂੰਹ (mūnh) — eye, ear, mouth. One more completes the face, and it closes the chapter on the cleanest English cousin this book has found yet.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਨੱਕ — nakk — nose.
ਨ n, ੱ the addak, ਕ k — the same doubling mark as ਅੱਖ (akkh), and for the same reason: nothing here was ever breathy, so nothing here traded itself for a tone.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — closing the chapter, and the tone table

segments.text: nakk is inherited from Old Punjabi naku, and its root is Proto-Indo- European neh₂s- — unbroken, all the way to English nose itself, Latin nāsus, and Lithuanian nósis. Like akkh, nakk needed no ship and no loanword to reach you, only the ordinary work of sound change and a doubled consonant that held its ground.

Run the whole face and its tone table: akkh flat, doubled; kann flat, nasal, no relation at all to karnā; mūnh level and high, a worn-down kh; nakk flat, doubled, the clean cousin of nose. Two of the four carry no tone because their old consonants survived whole; one carries a level high tone because its consonant vanished entirely; none of the four carries the low or falling tones you met on verbs and on bharā — those belong to words that opened or closed with a breathy voice, and nothing here ever did.
